title: The War Tehran Believes Is Coming
author: Jeremy Scahill
content:

walk past a banner depicting the portraits of Iran's former supreme leader

The U.S. and Israel are preparing to resume attacks on Iran, according to
senior Iranian officials and a U.S. official, and may even launch operations
before next week's Israeli elections. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is
fighting for his political life, and the Israeli press is rife with reports
that he is looking for a way to exploit the Iran standoff to his advantage. In
the U.S., President Donald Trump's approval ratings are at historic lows, and
the midterm elections are less than two weeks away.

Iran's top security official, Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, the Secretary of Iran's
Supreme National Security Council and personal representative of Supreme
Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, told Drop Site that, in the event of an
attack, Iran still has capacity to continue launching missiles and drones at
various U.S. assets across the region in retaliation and that it would expand
its range of targets.

"If the question is whether Iran still has the ability to continue missile and
drone operations, the answer is yes," Rezaei said in an exclusive written
interview. "The United States has valuable assets in the region. In the event
of war, cables, data centers and artificial intelligence facilities could also
come within range. If the conflict begins again, we will have a broader plan."

"Everyone must understand that action against Iran carries a cost," he added.
"If diplomacy can bring about that understanding, we prefer diplomacy. But if
the war continues, Iran has the tools it needs to keep responding."

A senior Iranian official told Drop Site that Tehran's current internal
intelligence assessment indicates a high likelihood that large-scale bombing
may even begin before Tuesday's Israeli elections. "Trump has sat on Iran's
proposed package for ending the war, and negotiations have stalled," said the
official, who is not authorized to speak publicly. "Contrary to the show he is
putting on, Trump has no clear or actionable plan for [ending] the war with
Iran. This has been the cause of a diplomatic deadlock." He warned that Iran
should not be underestimated, claiming, "Should another war against Iran
begin, given our knowledge of the patterns of American force deployment in the
countries of the region, their casualty figures will be ten times higher."

The White House denied it was planning to strike Iran in the next two weeks.
"The United States will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm
elections," White House Principal Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly said in a
statement to Drop Site.

Tehran believes Israel would be tasked with firing the first shots, the senior
Iranian official said, aimed at "destroying Iran's newly deployed air defense
systems, in order to open the path for American bombers." The U.S., he said,
would likely focus on attacking Iran's southern defense systems along the
Strait of Hormuz and potentially attempt to seize one of the islands off the
Iranian mainland after heavy bombing. Trump, he said, is continuing his quest
for a notable action that he can use to proclaim victory, adding that Iran
believes he may seek to launch a "token" attack on one of Iran's underground
nuclear sites, such as Pickaxe Mountain, and subsequently portray it as a
definitive blow. "Trump is flat-out lying about Iran's nuclear program," the
official said.

A U.S. official confirmed to Drop Site that military assets are being moved
rapidly into place in preparation for an expected green light from Trump.
Among the American officials pushing for renewed attacks is U.S. Central
Command chief Gen. Bradley Cooper, the official said. "CENTCOM is putting all
the pieces into place to renew major combat operations," added the official,
who is not authorized to discuss war plans. He was skeptical the war would
resume before the Israeli elections, but conceded, "We did start Epic Fury
without all our assets in place."

The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit are
[heading](https://x.com/jengriffinfnc/status/2112562701872283885?s=46) to the
Middle East, bringing approximately 10,000 additional sailors and Marines to
the region. The Roosevelt, which departed Japan on Monday, could reach the
region by the end of next week ahead of its initially expected deployment
slated for late November. It will join the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George
Washington, both currently in the Arabian Sea.

While the U.S. official said the likelihood of new U.S.-Israeli attacks was
high, he acknowledged that Trump has gone to the brink of military action and
pulled back more times than is publicly known. "Trump has backed off major
combat operations against Iran or the Houthis seven times since July," the
U.S. official said, referring to Ansarallah, who launched a major offensive
against Saudi-backed groups in Yemen. "At the last minute, he calls it off."

Netanyahu, who is behind in the polls, claimed Wednesday without evidence that
Iran was actively working on the development of a nuclear weapon and said he
had ordered the Israeli military to prepare for preemptive action. "The
Iranian regime still has not learned its lesson. Mojtaba Khamenei decided to
follow in his father's footsteps. He has taken off the safety, and Iran is
once again trying to develop its weapons of death," Netanyahu said. "There is
only one way to remove this threat once and for all, to topple the regime in
Iran, and that is my directive to the IDF, the Mossad and the security
agencies."

Analysts say that Trump is continuing to pursue an elusive clean victory
narrative, while Netanyahu understands this may be his last chance at
continuing the war he has agitated for his entire political career.

"This is Netanyahu's last chance to do so. And he's not going to leave until
he turns every stone to be able to achieve it. Particularly knowing that
either his career is going to end or the United States is going to go in a
direction in which this no longer will be an option," said Trita Parsi, a
leading Iran expert and the executive Vice President of the Quincy Institute.
"Trump, I suspect, has already made a decision that he's going to go to war,"
he added. "The Israelis have been very successful playing to his psychology,
which is that he's willing to take massive risks as long as he has the belief
that it can get him a victory so that he avoids accepting defeat, which is so
crucial for him. But it is a massive miscalculation that will make the
situation 100 times worse."

The intersection of Trump's and Netanyahu's political interests increases the
chances that the war will resume, argues former senior U.S. Iran negotiator
Robert Malley. "Netanyahu may want a longer campaign with broader objectives.
Trump may want something shorter that he could quickly get out of. The overlap
between the two might well be an intensive campaign that doesn't last too
long," said Malley, a key figure in brokering the 2015 Iran nuclear deal.
"President Trump may want a victory lap and an exit ramp. But as has been
proven time and time again, the exit is not decided by him alone," said
Malley, who currently directs the Middle East Program at the International
Crisis Group. "There is every reason to believe the Iranians are preparing all
kinds of steps, whether by them or by their regional partners, whether in or
out of theater, to ensure that however much he wants a victory lap and an exit
ramp, he is deprived of both."

## **" We Are Prepared for the Next Stage"**

Gen. Rezaei is one of the most prominent military figures in modern Iranian
history. A former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, he was
tapped to serve as the top military advisor to Khamenei in August. His
comments are often viewed as reflecting the consensus at the top of Iran's
power structure. He told Drop Site that despite U.S. claims to have
"obliterated" or "decimated" Iran's military infrastructure, Iran spent
decades preparing for a broader war waged by the U.S.

"Iran has invested for years in building redundancy into these capabilities:
dispersed production, underground facilities, different launch systems and the
ability to repair damage and replace losses," Rezaei told Drop Site. "More
importantly, you should not assess our capacity solely by asking how many
missiles remain in storage. In a prolonged war, the central question is
whether a country can sustain a continuous cycle of production, deployment and
response. We have shown that, even months after the war began, we can still
impose costs on the other side."

Rezaei also indicated that Tehran would deploy new capabilities in its
retaliatory response. "We did not deploy all our capabilities in the previous
stages. We brought more capabilities into operation in proportion to the
intensity of the war, and we are also prepared for the next stage," Rezaei
said.

During the war, Iran carried out at least 135 drone and missile strikes on 84
critical infrastructure sites across seven countries--Saudi Arabia, the UAE,
Iraq, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, and Bahrain, according to a [Reuters
investigation](https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/iran-
crisis-infrastructure-attacks/). While Gulf governments repeatedly attributed
the damage to falling debris from intercepted Iranian missiles and drones, the
investigation found evidence of deliberate, precision strikes targeting
critical equipment. The attacks demonstrated "precision, targeting expertise,
and patience," Ryan Stevens, a former U.S. Marine Corps special operations
airstrike coordinator, told Reuters.

Echoing Rezaei's warning about communications infrastructure, Iran's Islamic
Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson, Hossein Mohebi, also threatened to
target internet cables passing through the Strait of Hormuz if the U.S.
launched renewed attacks. Mohebi further
[warned](https://en.mehrnews.com/news/248723/World-to-face-serious-energy-
crisis-if-US-resumes-war-on-Iran) Monday that another U.S. military operation
would trigger a global energy crisis. "If America takes a new action--even a
limited one--the world will face a serious energy crisis," he told the Tehran
Times.

Rezaei did not rule out targeting energy infrastructure in Gulf states as a
retaliatory measure. "If the U.S. strategy is to prolong the war while using
neighboring countries' energy infrastructure to offset the pressure arising
from Hormuz and maintain the blockade of Iran, those governments should not
assume they can participate in economic warfare against Iran without putting
themselves at risk," he said. "The message is not that Iran wants to destroy
the Persian Gulf's energy system. The message is that there can be no
arrangement in which Iran's economic lifelines come under attack while the
economic architecture enabling those attacks is considered untouched and
immune."

The senior Iranian official said Trump's approach to Iran has been focused on
short-term objectives that are often disconnected from geopolitical realities
or core U.S. interests, likening him to a day trader. "The wartime secrecy
surrounding military operations has given him and his family exclusive and
extraordinary access to information regarding forthcoming actions and the
state of the markets--access that benefits only those closest to him," he
said. "Perpetuating the current situation will carry strategic consequences,
not least that the energy markets will not find calm for the next three years.
The continuation of this war has shifted the dynamics of relations in Iran's
favor, as the littoral states of the Persian Gulf are rapidly redefining their
relationship with Iran, having become convinced that the U.S. military is
incapable of defending its own bases, this at a time when those same states
had expected America to defend their countries."

Iranian officials have said repeatedly that Iran will not back away from its
red lines in any negotiations, consistently pointing to Tehran's acceptance of
the June 17 Memorandum of Understanding, which was swiftly violated by the
U.S., leading to a breakdown in the diplomatic process in early July.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he presented a "Seven-Day Plan"
to the U.S. through mediators at last month's UN General Assembly, outlining
steps for an end to the war and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. "Under
this proposal, the U.S. would not be expected to do anything that it has not
already agreed to," Araghchi
[wrote](https://www.ft.com/content/61bf9676-ea46-4956-b87f-6ab096accafa) in an
op-ed for the Financial Times on Wednesday. He said the framework's steps and
outcome were clear: "The Strait would reopen on Day 6, with the resumption of
talks for a final deal commencing on Day 7." Araghchi
[claimed](https://en.irna.ir/news/86298957/US-accepted-Iran-s-seven-day-
proposal-but-sought-additional-terms) in an interview with Iraqi television
that the U.S. had accepted the seven-day proposal but requested the addition
of a "few more clauses," adding that diplomatic contacts through mediators
remain ongoing.

"As President Trump stated, Iran is in very bad condition, both economically
and militarily, and the blockade will remain in full force and effect, with
oil flowing in record numbers of barrels through the Hormuz Strait," Kelly
told Drop Site in a statement.

Rezaei told Drop Site that Iran's negotiating strategy has evolved as a result
of Trump's unreliability. "We will not return to our previous approach to
diplomacy, but we will not abandon diplomacy either. We have presented seven
new conditions through intermediaries. Until those conditions are fulfilled,
Iran will neither reopen the strait nor return to negotiations," Rezaei said.
"The first memorandum failed because the commitments were implemented in the
wrong order. We opened the strait and maritime traffic resumed, but the other
side's political and economic commitments were not implemented in a way that
could sustain the agreement. Once the United States obtained what it
immediately needed, the balance of leverage shifted. That experience matters
to us."

"If Washington honors its commitments, there is a path to reopening the Strait
of Hormuz and continuing diplomacy," he continued. "But Iran will not first
give up the leverage that brought the other side to the negotiating table and
then wait to see whether its promises are fulfilled."

Parsi said that Iran is not eager to resume the war, but has recognized that
the diplomatic track has been treated by the U.S. as an ultimatum operation
masquerading as negotiations. "Their conclusion--based on extensive experience
with Trump now--is that he simply won't back off unless his policy is reaching
a cost to him that is intolerable. And that it's not concessions or face
saving exits that will get Trump to back off, but simply that the policy
becomes too costly."

Attacks on ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz have surged to a record
high in recent weeks, with more than two dozen vessels reporting attacks so
far in October, according to data released Friday by the UK Maritime Trade
Operations agency. The agency said the actual number was likely far higher, as
the "majority of vessels attacked" were refusing to report incidents.

The IRGC reported further attacks over the weekend and into Tuesday, including
a supertanker carrying two million barrels of oil struck Saturday, another
tanker hit Sunday, and two tankers that it said caught fire Tuesday after
striking naval mines south of the Strait. Iran says it is targeting vessels
violating its maritime restrictions or using unauthorized shipping routes.

"Over the past two or three months, we have struck an average of five vessels
belonging to these smugglers every night," Rezaei said. "Smuggling is taking
place along the southern edge of the strait at enormous cost and with
considerable risk. Trump then says the Strait of Hormuz is open."

Despite the escalating attacks, oil exports from the Middle East appear to
have rebounded past prewar levels, primarily through tanker-to-tanker
transfers in the Gulf of Oman, and expanded use of Saudi and Emirati pipelines
bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. However, oil prices remain high, hovering well
above $100 per barrel of Brent crude amid fears of the ongoing attacks and
diminishing U.S. fuel stockpiles. "The current price of oil reflects the
reality," Rezaei said.

"The management of Hormuz is a national asset for us, and this is not simply
about collecting tolls. The main issue is security," he continued. "Charges
can also be collected for security, insurance and environmental costs, but the
importance of managing the strait goes far beyond the revenue it generates,"
he said. "We will continue managing it to maintain peace and security in the
region, and we will not back down from this position."

The senior Iranian official said that the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz
"has become the new pretext--the nuclear issue, previously, was a lie upon
which the war was launched--for the United States to prolong the war." Trump,
he charged, "has fallen into the trap of prolonging what was advertised as the
shortest of wars." A "war of attrition," he said, "will work to Iran's
advantage and to America's detriment."

The war has had a devastating impact on Iran's economy. As part of its
escalation over the summer, the U.S. reimposed a blockade on Iran's southern
ports and launched a new campaign of sanctions dubbed Operation Economic
Outcast. The Iranian rial subsequently collapsed, falling to record lows,
making imports dramatically more expensive and imposing even more scarcity on
people in Iran.

"Iran will suffer from a prolonged blockade; anyone who says otherwise is not
being realistic. Families will bear the costs, investment will suffer, and
sustaining some sectors of the economy will become more difficult. But
economic pain and strategic collapse are not the same thing," Rezaei said.
"Washington has repeatedly made the mistake of assuming that, if it can make
life inside Iran difficult enough, Iran's political system will consequently
accept America's strategic demands. These are two different calculations."

"Our goal is not to make it to 2029. Our goal is to end the war on terms that
reduce the likelihood of another war."
